name: Zoe Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the stock manager at the Kowalskis' farm, which rears calves for beef, about five hundred a year, and grows sugar beet and barley. My mornings are the calf sheds: milk feeding, checking for scours, which is a bad stomach bug calves get, and moving the older ones on. Afternoons I help wherever I'm needed, and in October that's beet lifting until dark. It's a good job, it pays well, and Mr Kowalski leaves me to it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what keeps you going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Losing a calf wears me out, every single time, even after ten years around them. What keeps me going is that I'm learning how a bigger place runs, because my parents have their own farm three miles away and one day I'll go back and take it on. Dad says I'm on an apprenticeship that pays better than his.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about home and about technology.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Ben, my partner, he's a builder, mostly extensions and barn conversions. We've got savings, a good bit more than six months, and Dad's put me into the family farm partnership, so I own a small share of that. I use AI now and then, for checking market prices or filling in grant forms. I didn't trust it at first, but Ben's sister uses it for everything and it hasn't killed her yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not shocked. Farming always has a new thing every few years that's going to change everything, and usually it changes a bit. I'd say the old ways are the old ways for a reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, that's fine. I'd carry on with the Kowalskis for a few more years, then go home to the family farm when Dad's ready to step back. The plan I've always had still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving with Ben. Maybe start looking at a plot on Dad's land to build a house on, since Ben could do most of the work himself. Keep using the AI for the grant forms, because it does save a morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad nothing's being shaken up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far off is going home to the family farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four or five years, probably. Dad's fifty-eight and his back's going, but he won't admit it. Mum does the books, and she's already asked me twice when I'm coming home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Ben build the house himself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd want to. He's built extensions for half the village and never had a proper place of his own. It's the thing he talks about most when we're walking the dog.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not shocked, because farming has a new thing every few years that only changes a bit. The old ways are the old ways for a reason.
S0.think: For me that's fine, because the plan I've always had still works. I'd stay with my employer a few more years, then go home to take on the family farm.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving with her partner. Starts looking at a plot on her father's land for a house her builder partner could build, and keeps using AI for grant forms.
S0.feel: Calm and glad nothing's being shaken up.
S0.quote: He's built extensions for half the village and never had a proper place of his own.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe has a clear plan rooted in family: learn on a bigger farm, then take over her parents' place. She uses AI cautiously and only where it plainly saves time. The house her partner wants to build is the next piece of the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers who get ready will be fine, and it's up to each of us to get ready. Nobody's going to do it for us. I'd say it at the young farmers' club, probably over a pint.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about Dad's farm more than my job. A small farm with a hundred and twenty acres can't afford the robots, and the big places that can will make everything cheaper. I'd be fine at the Kowalskis', but the plan of going home might not add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the Kowalskis bring in and learn it properly there, on their money, before Dad has to spend his. Then I'd sit down with Dad and Mum and go through the numbers on whether the home farm needs to change, maybe go more into the calves, since I know that side. I wouldn't rush anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why learn on the Kowalskis' money first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if it's rubbish, I'd rather it was their mistake than Dad's. Mr Kowalski can afford a bad year. Dad can't, not really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's up to each of us to get ready. Does that include your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's the hard bit. He'd say he's farmed thirty years without a computer. I'd have to show him, not tell him, or he'd dig his heels in.

S1.say: I'd say farmers who get ready will be fine, and it's up to each of us, because nobody's going to do it for us. I'd say it at the young farmers' club over a pint.
S1.think: I'd worry about my dad's small farm more than my own job, because big farms with robots will make everything cheaper. My plan of going home might not add up any more.
S1.do: Learns new kit on her employer's farm first, so any mistakes aren't her father's. Then goes through the home farm's numbers with her parents and considers shifting it towards calf rearing.
S1.quote: Mr Kowalski can afford a bad year. Dad can't, not really.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is for the family farm rather than her own wages. She plans to learn on her employer's money as a deliberate way to protect her father. Her belief in self-reliance applies to her own family too, which she finds hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happened, so there's no point moaning, we have to deal with it. I'd want the government to stay out of the way and let farmers sort themselves out. Though I'd probably change my mind if it got bad enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years would wreck the plan. The Kowalskis would buy robots for the calves and the beet, and Dad's farm couldn't keep up with what big places can sell for. I'd have savings and Ben would still have building work for a bit, but I'd lose the future I've been working towards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home straight away rather than in five years, to help Dad and Mum work out what to do while there's still time. We'd pool what we have, my savings and theirs, and decide whether to buy one robot together or sell some land. Ben and I would put the house off and move into the old farm cottage to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy, but my chest would be tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the government should stay out of it, then said you might change your mind. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, if I'm honest. I don't like handouts. But if it was the whole country losing work in two years, I'm not too proud to say we'd need something. I'd just want it to be help to work, not help to sit still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with the slower versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means Dad and I make the decision together in a hurry, and that's when families fall out. With ten years, I'd take over gradually and we'd do it properly. It's the speed that would hurt, more than the robots.

S2.say: I'd say it's happened, so there's no point moaning and we have to deal with it. I'd want the government to stay out and let farmers sort themselves out, though I might change my mind if it got bad enough.
S2.think: Two years would wreck my plan, because big farms would automate and my dad's farm couldn't keep up on price. I'd have savings, but I'd lose the future I've been working towards.
S2.do: Goes home to the family farm straight away to help her parents decide what to do. Pools savings with them to decide on buying one robot or selling land, puts off building a house and moves into the old farm cottage to save rent.
S2.feel: Anxious, busy but with a tight chest.
S2.quote: Two years means Dad and I make the decision together in a hurry, and that's when families fall out.
S2.fieldNote: Her first move is towards family, not away. She admitted her dislike of state help might bend if the whole country were hit, but wants it to be help to work. She sees the speed, not the technology, as the real danger to her family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now and stop waiting for someone else to fix it. Farm families should be talking tonight, not next year. I'd say that more firmly than I'd say most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to go home properly and help change the farm before 2031. I think we could make it work if we picked one thing and did it really well, like calf rearing. It's still a gamble, but it's our gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd learn every bit of kit the Kowalskis bring in, and do a short course on the robot feeders. Then I'd go home in year two or three, and help Dad buy one proven machine, probably a calf feeder, out of the family savings. Ben and I would build the house a bit later than planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It feels like hard work, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your dad accept a robot feeder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I showed him one working at the Kowalskis', with the calves growing well, yes. He's stubborn, but he's not daft. He bought a quad bike after seeing the neighbour's for three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would Ben's work look like in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks builders are safe for a good while because every job's different. I'm not so sure, but he'd have a few years at least. If his work slowed down, he'd help on the farm, he's handier than he lets on.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now and stop waiting for someone else to fix it. Farm families should be talking tonight, not next year.
S3.think: Five years gives me time to go home properly and change the farm before 2031, maybe by focusing on calf rearing. It's still a gamble, but it's our gamble.
S3.do: Learns all new kit on her employer's farm in the first year and takes a short course on robot feeders. Goes home in year two or three to help her father buy one proven calf feeder from family savings, and delays building the house.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steady, more hard work than disaster.
S3.quote: He bought a quad bike after seeing the neighbour's for three years.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she can follow her usual pattern: see it proven, then adopt. She plans to win her father over by showing rather than telling. Her partner's work is a back-up she half trusts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and anyone who isn't ready by 2036 has had their chance. That sounds hard, but I'd mean it kindly. I'd also say young people should be doing apprenticeships, not just sitting on phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I think I'd come out fine. I'd take over from Dad gradually, bring in the machines once they've been proven elsewhere, and still be the one running the place. Whether there's a family farm left for my own children is another question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick to the plan: a few more years at the Kowalskis', then home. Ben and I would build the house on Dad's land, probably start in two years. I'd wait and see which robots really work on small farms, then buy one or two with Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of worry about the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your own children. Is that part of the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, Ben and I want them, maybe in three or four years. I'd want them to grow up on a farm like I did, bottle-feeding calves before school. Even if robots did the work, I'd want them to know how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does more time change anything about who you'd blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame myself, honestly, if I'd had ten years and not got ready. With two years I'd blame whoever let it happen that fast. With ten, it's on us.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning, and anyone not ready by 2036 has had their chance, though I'd mean it kindly. Young people should be doing apprenticeships, not just sitting on phones.
S4.think: With ten years I think I'd come out fine, taking over from my dad gradually and bringing in proven machines. Whether there's a family farm left for my own children is another question.
S4.do: Sticks to her plan of a few more years at her current job before going home. Builds a house on her father's land with her partner in about two years and buys one or two proven robots with her father.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with some worry about the long run.
S4.quote: With two years I'd blame whoever let it happen that fast. With ten, it's on us.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep her original plan almost intact. Her sense of who's to blame shifts with the warning time, from outsiders to herself. Children growing up on the farm are central to what she's protecting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would force Dad and me into a rushed decision about the farm. What would help is good apprenticeships and help for small family farms to buy proven machines, loans rather than handouts. And time, really, just time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the family farms, not just the jobs. If my generation can't take them on, they'll all be sold to the big places. Then it doesn't matter who works there, robots or people, because nobody local owns anything any more.

headlineQuote: Then it doesn't matter who works there, robots or people, because nobody local owns anything any more.
portrait: Zoe Bauer, 27, is stock manager at a calf-rearing and arable farm and plans to take over her parents' small farm a few miles away. She lives with her partner Ben, a builder, owns a share in the family farm partnership, and uses AI now and then for market prices and grant forms. She's calm about the AI Plateau and uneasy for her father's farm under Steady Disruption. AGI by 2028 makes her anxious enough to move home at once, while with more time she'd follow her usual pattern of waiting until a machine is proven, then buying it with her dad.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because it would force her and her father into a rushed decision about the family farm.
whatWouldHelp: Good apprenticeships, loans rather than handouts to help small family farms buy proven machines, and time.
